note: The Tribune, 11 March 1905: Mrs. Catherine G. Brown, 'former wife of Charles E. Brown, 1612 Prairie avenue', 27, 'the daughter of Gen. Graves, a wealthy resident of Buffalo', first attracted notoriety in May 1904 when her husband filed for divorce; 'By a court order issued by Judge Tuley Mrs. Brown was given possession of the residence, 1612 Prairie avenue, where she and her husband and their son had lived, and was granted temporary alimony amounting to $200 a month while the suit was pending'; 'In November Mr. Brown appeared in court and charged that his wife had conducted herself in a disgraceful manner, had been habitually intoxicated, and had done many freakish things, such as playing a violin in a broken automobile while a man pushed the machine along a public highway, and dancing about the rear of their home clothed only in a nightrobe'; he charged her with 'receiving the attentions of E. C. Edsall, an automobile salesman', with whom she 'ran away to an eastern summer resort and later to New York City'; 'After a bitter fight Mr. Brown was granted a divorce about six weeks ago, and given possession of the Prairie avenue property, and the custody of the one son, Charles Edward Brown'. In March 1905 she was arrested at 3667 Wabash, where she lived 'under the name of Kittie Casey, according to the police', fined $85 ('I am penniless,' she said. 'I cannot pay the fine.'), and said 'It's all because a woman is jealous of me, I guess.' The 14 March 1905 transfers: 1612 Prairie, March 8, Chas. S. [sic] Brown to the Rt. Rev. Chas. Palmerston Anderson, bishop. The 22 February 1884 Tribune: a reception for about 200 at W. F. Studebaker's, No. 1612 Prairie, the house 'brilliantly illuminated', every room 'elaborately decorated with smilax and cut flowers'. The allegations in the divorce are one side's, and the arrest's charges the police's and the complainants'.
